title: The priest and the big bang
hookLine: Georges Lemaître, a Belgian priest and physicist, proposed the expanding universe

cards: A man in a black clerical collar stands at a blackboard covered in equations. He's a Catholic priest, and also a physicist, trained in the mathematics of Einstein's theory of gravity.
And the equations are telling him something strange. The universe isn't standing still. It's getting bigger.
Run the film backward, he reasons, and everything gets closer and closer together, until it all begins from one small, dense starting point. He called it a primeval atom.
Other people later gave it a nickname, and the nickname stuck. His name was Georges Lemaître, a Belgian priest.

teach.b: The first line of the Bible, in the King James translation: "In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth." A few lines later: "And God said, Let there be light: and there was light."
It would be easy to hear Lemaître's idea, a universe with a beginning, and say: Genesis, proved by physics. Lemaître himself didn't want anyone to say that.
When church voices began to treat his theory as scientific proof of creation, he pushed back, quietly but firmly.

His reasoning, as it's usually reported: physics describes how the universe unfolds; it can't tell you whether there is a God. And the Bible wasn't written to teach science; it was written to teach the way to salvation.
Keep the two in their own lanes, and neither has to be afraid of the other. He spent his life in both. He said Mass and did mathematics, and didn't think he was being torn in half.

Christians have held a range of views on faith and science, and still do. Some read Genesis as a literal account of how the world was made. Others read it as a different kind of truth, about who made the world and why.
Lemaître's own path was to study the heavens as closely as he could, and to keep praying.

teach.h: THE HEAVENS DECLARE THE GLORY OF GOD.
teach.b: An old psalm sits well beside his blackboard: "The heavens declare the glory of God; and the firmament sheweth his handywork." The psalm doesn't do the math. It looks up, and it praises.

how: Christians hold a range of views on how scripture and science fit together; the Catholic Church has its own academy of sciences, and Christians work as scientists across many fields.

games.q: you're a priest-physicist, and church voices start saying your theory proves the Bible. what do you do?
o: welcome it: the theory proves Genesis.
push back: physics can't prove or disprove God.
drop the theory to avoid trouble.
games.why: Lemaître pushed back. physics describes how the universe unfolds; the Bible, he said, teaches the way to salvation.

practice: Find the sky you have, the night through a window, the daylight and clouds, or the last starry night you remember, and let your eyes go as far as they can; far beyond what you can see, Lemaître would say, the universe is still growing.
If you pray, say the psalm's line, the heavens declare the glory of God; if not, simply look, and let yourself be small for a while.

wordCard.voice: Firmament. The King James word for the sky's dome, named in the psalm that watched beside Georges Lemaître's blackboard as he studied a universe with a beginning.

orig.note: Hebrew: the firmament, the spread-out sky — "the firmament sheweth his handywork" in Psalm 19:1.

carryVoice: Your line: faith and science. One priest kept a blackboard and a prayer book both. Day nine hundred eighty-eight.
